question: Article 10 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union guarantees freedom of thought, conscience and religion, and recognises the right to refuse to act contrary to one’s own conscience, in accordance with national legislation. Article 21 prohibits discrimination on grounds including religion or belief.

The Commission has developed instruments and strategies to combat anti-Semitism and hatred towards Muslims. At the same time, there is no comparable, systematic mechanism for monitoring acts of hatred, discrimination and violence against Christians. This therefore raises the question of ensuring an equal standard of protection for all religious communities. 1.

Does the Commission intend to establish a systematic mechanism for monitoring and countering acts of hate, violence and discrimination against Christians, comparable to the instruments in place for other religious communities? If not, why not?

Does the Commission consider that Directive 2000/78/EC provides sufficient protection for employees invoking conscientious objection, in particular in the medical professions and other situations where professional duties may come into conflict with religious beliefs?

Does the Commission plan to issue guidelines or take other measures to ensure an appropriate balance between the principle of non-discrimination and freedom of conscience and religion in the workplace?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (25.11.2026) 1. The Commission is aware of the instances of hatred, discrimination and violence targeting Christians. Through its policy instruments to address hate speech and hate crime, the Commission is addressing and monitoring closely the situation as regards hate based on religion within the EU, including against Christians.

The Commission cooperates with the Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights which provides regular data on hate crimes targeting Christians1, in the context of the Commission’s High-Level Group on combating hate speech and hate crime. According to the data available, most of the attacks against Christians are targeting places of worship.

The Commission has adopted an Action Plan to support the protection of public spaces2. In this context, the Commission provides funding to ensure the protection of places of worship across the EU, by promoting security awareness, the role of religious communities in preventing risks and enhanced relations with law enforcement officials to prevent and counter threats effectively. 2.

Council Directive 2000/78/EC prohibits discrimination in employment and occupation where based on inter alia religion or belief3. The Directive must be interpreted in the light of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the European Union including its Article 10(1), and of the case law of the Court of Justice of the European Union on the matter4.

In July 2026, the Commission published the most recent report on the application of the Directive5. 3. The priority of the Commission is to ensure the full implementation of the Directive in all the Member States.
1 https://hatecrime.osce.org/hate-crime-report. 2 COM(2017) 612 final, 18.10.2017. 3 Council Directive 2000/78/EC of 27 November 2000 establishing a general framework for equal treatment in

employment and occupation, OJ L 303, 2.12.2000, p. 16–22, https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legalcontent/EN/TXT/?uri=celex%3A32000L0078. 4 Judgement of 17 March 2026, Case C-258/24, Katholische Schwangerschaftsberatung, ECLI:EU:C:2026:211.

5 Report from the Commission to the European Parliament and the Council on the application of Council Directive 2000/43/EC implementing the principle of equal treatment between persons irrespective of racial or ethnic origin (the Racial Equality Directive) and of Council Directive 2000/78/EC establishing a general framework for equal treatment in employment and occupation (the Employment Equality Directive), COM/2026/364 final.
